hints: Think about where silicon sits in Period 3 and whether its chloride is ionic like magnesium chloride or molecular like carbon tetrachloride.
Recall what colour most pure covalent chlorides of Period 3 have and what type of forces between molecules this implies for state at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Picture SiCl4 at room temperature**
Silicon forms four strong covalent bonds to chlorine to give discrete $\text{SiCl}_4$ molecules. There are no ions and no giant lattice, so you get a volatile liquid, not a high melting solid. Pure samples are colourless liquids.

Name the structure type correctly**
Because it exists as separate neutral molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces, describe it as simple molecular. The bonding within each molecule is covalent by sharing of electrons between $\text{Si}$ and $\text{Cl}$.

Final answer: appearance: colourless liquid
structure and bonding: simple molecular, covalent

hints: Recall the starting solids: both $\text{MgCl}_2$ and $\text{PCl}_5$ are white solids at room temperature.
Think about what happens when any chloride dissolves or reacts: both will give a colourless solution, but only one reacts violently to release acid gas.
Remember that $\text{HCl}$ gas in moist air forms white misty fumes, so ask which chloride hydrolyses fully to give $\text{HCl}$.
Link the strength of hydrolysis to pH: slightly acidic from hydrated $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ versus strongly acidic from $\text{HCl}$ and phosphoric acid.
walkthrough:
Start from the solids**
At room temperature both chlorides are white crystalline solids. $\text{PCl}_5$ samples often look pale yellow due to slight dissociation, but white is accepted. This is just observation before water is added.

Spot what is the same on adding water**
Both solids disappear to give a colourless solution. For $\text{MgCl}_2$ this is mainly dissolving with slight hydrolysis. For $\text{PCl}_5$ this is vigorous full hydrolysis: $\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$.

Spot the key visible difference**
Only the vigorous hydrolysis releases $\text{HCl(g)}$ which mixes with moisture in air to give white misty or steamy fumes. So $\text{PCl}_5$ shows fumes, $\text{MgCl}_2$ shows no fumes, just a clear solution.

Predict the pH**
$\text{MgCl}_2$ solution contains $\text{[Mg(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$ which hydrolyses very slightly, so pH is only weakly acidic, about 6.5 to 7. $\text{PCl}_5$ produces strong acid $\text{HCl}$ plus $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, so pH is strongly acidic, 0 to 4.

Final answer: appearance: $\text{MgCl}_2$ white solid / crystals; $\text{PCl}_5$ white or pale yellow solid / crystals
similarity: colourless solution formed in both
difference: $\text{MgCl}_2$ no misty fumes; $\text{PCl}_5$ misty / steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$
pH: $\text{MgCl}_2$ approx 6.5 to 7; $\text{PCl}_5$ 0 to 4

hints: Remember that chlorine with cold dilute alkali gives chlorate(I), while hotter concentrated conditions push oxidation further to chlorate(V).
walkthrough:
Choose hot alkali for chlorate(V)**
Chlorine disproportionates with alkali in two ways. Cold dilute $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ gives $\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. To get sodium chlorate(V), $\text{NaClO}_3$, you need hot concentrated $\text{NaOH(aq)}$. The heat favours formation of the +5 oxidation state: $3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Final answer: hot aqueous sodium hydroxide, $\text{NaOH(aq)}$

hints: Track the oxidation number of chlorine starting at 0 in $\text{Cl}_2$ and see whether it goes up in one product and down in the other.
walkthrough:
Show simultaneous oxidation and reduction**
Disproportionation means the same element is both oxidised and reduced. Here $\text{Cl}_2$ has oxidation number 0. In $\text{Cl}^-$ it becomes -1, a decrease so reduction. In $\text{ClO}_3^-$ it becomes +5, an increase so oxidation. One species doing both makes it disproportionation.
Final answer: Chlorine is both oxidised from 0 to +5 in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and reduced from 0 to -1 in $\text{Cl}^-$

hints: Think about what energy source is needed to split the strong $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond into radicals to start the chain with an alkane.
walkthrough:
Provide energy for homolysis**
Alkanes do not react with chlorine in the dark at room temperature. Ultraviolet light provides the energy for homolytic fission of $\text{Cl}_2$ into $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals, which then attack methane. Heat at high temperature can also initiate, but uv light is the standard AS condition.
Final answer: ultraviolet light / uv / sunlight

hints: Start by writing the homolysis of chlorine that supplies $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ for every chain.

For propagation, let $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ abstract H from $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$ to make $\text{HCl}$ plus a new carbon radical, then that radical reacts with $\text{Cl}_2$ in a second step, but here only the first propagation forming $\text{CHCl}_2^\bullet$ is required.
For termination to give $\text{CHCl}_3$, combine the two radicals present so no new radical is produced.
walkthrough:
Write initiation**
Initiation always creates radicals from a molecule. Show homolytic fission with a single headed fishhook logic, written as: $$\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^\bullet$$ One $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond breaks to give two chlorine radicals.

Write the propagation that consumes CH2Cl2**
A $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ abstracts a hydrogen atom: $$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2 + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_2^\bullet + \text{HCl}$$ A radical is used and a new carbon radical $\text{CHCl}_2^\bullet$ is made, so the chain continues. The dot must be on the carbon radical product.

Write termination to CHCl3**
Termination removes radicals by combining them: $$\text{CHCl}_2^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_3$$ Two radicals join to make a stable molecule with no dots left. This directly builds trichloromethane.

Final answer: initiation: $\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^\bullet$
propagation: $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2 + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_2^\bullet + \text{HCl}$
termination: $\text{CHCl}_2^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_3$

hints: Count how many Cl atoms in $\text{CHCl}_3$ are replaced by F to make $\text{CHClF}_2$ and balance the $\text{HCl}$ formed with the $\text{HF}$ used.
walkthrough:
Balance the F for Cl swap**
Two fluorine atoms enter the organic molecule to give $\text{CHClF}_2$, so two $\text{HF}$ molecules are needed. The two displaced $\text{Cl}$ atoms leave with the two $\text{H}$ atoms as $2\text{HCl}$: $$\text{CHCl}_3 + 2\text{HF} \rightarrow \text{CHClF}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$$ Check atoms: C 1, H 1+2=3 on each side, Cl 3, F 2. Balanced.

hints: Work out the identity of X from substitution of H in $\text{CHClF}_2$ by Br, then calculate its lightest mass using $^{35}\text{Cl}$, $^{79}\text{Br}$ and $^{19}\text{F}$.
Remember both Cl and Br have two isotopes two mass units apart, so m/e 166 can arise in two different isotopic ways.
walkthrough:
Identify X and its lightest ion**
Substitution of the H in $\text{CHClF}_2$ by $\text{Br}_2$ gives $\text{CBrClF}_2$. Using $^{12}\text{C} + 2 \times ^{19}\text{F} + ^{35}\text{Cl} + ^{79}\text{Br} = 12 + 38 + 35 + 79 = 164$. So the 164 peak is $(\text{CF}_2{}^{35}\text{Cl}{}^{79}\text{Br})^+$.

Explain the 166 peak with two combinations**
Both chlorine ($^{35}\text{Cl}$:$^{37}\text{Cl}$) and bromine ($^{79}\text{Br}$:$^{81}\text{Br}$) have M and M+2 isotopes. Adding 2 mass units to 164 can be done either by heavy Cl with light Br or light Cl with heavy Br. So 166 contains both $(\text{CF}_2{}^{37}\text{Cl}{}^{79}\text{Br})^+$ and $(\text{CF}_2{}^{35}\text{Cl}{}^{81}\text{Br})^+$. The 168 peak given confirms the heaviest pair $(\text{CF}_2{}^{37}\text{Cl}{}^{81}\text{Br})^+.$

Final answer: m/e 164: $(\text{CF}_2{}^{35}\text{Cl}{}^{79}\text{Br})^+$
m/e 166: $(\text{CF}_2{}^{37}\text{Cl}{}^{79}\text{Br})^+$ and $(\text{CF}_2{}^{35}\text{Cl}{}^{81}\text{Br})^+$
